2. Disjoint perturbation supports do not factor through the coupled background

A source expansion cannot declare two perturbations independent merely because their supports are disjoint.

Take two adjacent qubits with

 $H=JX_1X_2,\qquad \gamma=1,\qquad
\rho_0=I/4,$ and

 $\mathcal D_i=\frac12(\mathcal R_{0,i}-\mathrm{Id}),
\qquad
\mathcal R_{0,i}(X)
=|0\rangle\langle0|_i\otimes\operatorname{Tr}_iX.$ These are rational permitted generators with diamond norm at most one.

Let  $a(t)$  be the coefficient of  $\eta_i$  in  $\langle Z_i\rangle_t$ . Its first-response equations are

 $a'=-a+2Jw+\frac12,\qquad
w'=-2Ja-2w,$ with zero initial data. Consequently,

 $a(t)=\frac t2-\frac{t^2}{4}
+\frac{1-4J^2}{12}t^3+O(t^4).$ The coefficient  $c(t)$  of  $\eta_1\eta_2$  in  $\langle Z_1Z_2\rangle_t$  obeys

 $c'=-2c+a,$ so

 $c(t)=\frac{t^2}{4}-\frac{t^3}{4}
+\frac{7-4J^2}{48}t^4+O(t^5).$ Subtracting the product of the first responses gives

 $\boxed{
[\eta_1\eta_2]\operatorname{Cov}_t(Z_1,Z_2)
=\frac{J^2t^4}{4}+O(t^5).
}
\tag{7}$ The source supports are disjoint, but their connected coefficient is nonzero. A valid resummation must include Hamiltonian-mediated connections. This is a failure of that proposed factorization, with no sampling-hardness implication.
